sections.h2: What is Will County, Illinois, and which offices touch a property tax bill?
sections.html:
Will County is a collar county southwest of Chicago, 849 square miles with Joliet as the seat and largest city. It was formed on January 12, 1836, out of Cook and Iroquois counties, and the 2020 census counted 696,355 residents, which made it the fourth most populous county in Illinois. The Du Page, Des Plaines and Kankakee rivers cross it, and the Midewin National Tallgrass Prairie covers about 17,000 acres on the former Joliet Arsenal grounds.

Four offices shape a bill. The Treasurer and the Board of Review both work out of the Will County Office Building at 302 N. Chicago Street in Joliet.

  • The Treasurer collects payments, runs the annual tax sale and mails the bills.
  • The Supervisor of Assessments works with the township assessors who set values.
  • The Board of Review, on the second floor, hears assessment complaints.
  • The County Clerk takes redemption payments after a tax sale.

Cities in the county include Joliet, Aurora, Naperville, Lockport, Crest Hill, Braidwood and Wilmington, while villages range from Bolingbrook, Plainfield and Romeoville to Frankfort, Mokena, New Lenox and Peotone. Several of those straddle county lines, so confirm which county bills a given parcel.

sections.h2: How do Will County housing costs compare with the rest of the country?
sections.html:
Will County's median home value for 2020 to 2024 was $319,600, a little under the national median of $332,700. Owners hold 82.8% of homes, and median household income is $109,984.

Commutes average 31.4 minutes, against 26.4 nationally. Four Metra lines and Amtrak at Joliet connect the county with downtown Chicago, and I-55, I-57, I-80 and I-355 cross it.

sections.h2: When does Will County property tax become late?
sections.html:
Illinois law makes the first installment delinquent after the later of June 1 or the day after the first due date printed on the bill. The second installment follows the same rule using September 1 and its printed date. Will County has fewer than 3,000,000 residents, so unpaid taxes bear interest of 1.5% per month or portion of a month (35 ILCS 200/21-15).

A mailed payment postmarked on or before the due date is not delinquent under that statute. If a mortgage lender holding enough escrow money lets a bill go late, the interest falls on the lender rather than the borrower. Check the escrow account before you assume a bill was paid.

The Treasurer also offers e-notices, a free paperless bill. You enroll at enoticesonline.com with the authorization code on your latest bill, and paper bills stop once you do. If you lost the code, the Treasurer's office can reissue it.

sections.h2: Where and how can Will County taxes be paid?
sections.html:
The Treasurer lists several options beyond the online portal, and checks cost nothing extra.

  • By mail to 302 N. Chicago St., Joliet, IL 60432, payable to the Will County Treasurer. Add a stamped, self-addressed envelope for a receipt.
  • At more than 100 local bank branches that take part in the county program.
  • By phone at 815-680-2953, free when funds come from a checking or savings account. Other forms of payment carry convenience fees.
  • At the Treasurer's office with cash, check or credit card. Subsequent taxes are taken in the office only, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.
  • In the secure drop box at the Will County Building for after-hours checks.

sections.h2: How do Will County assessment complaints work?
sections.html:
The Board of Review hears complaints, and for 2026 the window ran from August 12 through September 14. The state rule sets 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published (35 ILCS 200/16-55), and the county opens its process each August. The Board suggests talking with your township assessor first about any change in value.

Each owner files a separate complaint for each parcel unless the parcels touch and share the same land use. The form needs the parcel number, the address, a signature, a mailing address and a daytime phone number. The Board's office is at 302 N. Chicago Street, second floor, and the phone is (815) 740-4707.

Hearings have their own rules. The Board asks you to check its portal 48 hours before the hearing to confirm that it is live, visitors pass a security check at the building, and a late arrival cannot be rescheduled. It weighs the cost, market and income approaches, so bring comparable sales or an appraisal.

sections.h2: Which exemptions apply in Will County?
sections.html:
Will County borders Cook County, so the higher dollar caps in the state code apply here.

  • General homestead exemption: up to $8,000 off equalized assessed value in counties contiguous to a county of 3,000,000 or more (35 ILCS 200/15-175).
  • Senior citizens exemption: up to $8,000 for owners 65 and older, under the same contiguity rule (35 ILCS 200/15-170).
  • Low-income senior assessment freeze (35 ILCS 200/15-172), with its own income test.

The county's property tax pages list exemptions and deferrals, and the Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Act is a separate route for older owners. When a homestead sells, the exemption continues for the rest of that assessment year, and the assessor may require the new owner to apply again.

sections.h2: What happens at the Will County tax sale, and can an owner redeem?
sections.html:
Under Illinois law, property with delinquent taxes carries a lien, and the delinquent taxes are sold to investors called tax buyers at the annual sale. Buyers bid on the interest rate they want, and the lowest bid wins. The buyer purchases a lien against the property, not the home.

The Treasurer's page says homeowners typically have one to three years from the sale to redeem before a buyer can start court action. The statute gives three years from the date of sale, with exceptions (35 ILCS 200/21-350). The County Clerk's tax redemption department takes redemption payments, typically beginning one to two weeks after the sale.

The county posts tax sale information for property owners and subsequent tax instructions on the Treasurer's annual tax sales page. Read that page before you list a house that has been behind on tax.

sections.h2: How should a Will County seller handle taxes at closing?
sections.html:
Order a payoff from the Treasurer and ask the title company to confirm every open year. A sold lien needs redemption through the County Clerk, so the title agent should check for one.

  • Pull the parcel number from the bill and confirm the township.
  • Check whether a general homestead or senior exemption is on the bill, and tell the buyer.
  • Pay open installments and any 1.5% monthly interest from the proceeds.
  • Record the deed with the Recorder of Deeds, whose fee schedule and transfer tax rules are covered on the county recorder page.

An inherited property or one with tenants adds title work, and unpaid tax can hold up the closing. Raise it with the closing agent at the start.

faqs.q: When are Will County property taxes late?
faqs.a: The first installment is delinquent after the later of June 1 or the day after the date printed on the bill, and the second after the later of September 1 or its printed date. Interest runs at 1.5% per month or part of a month.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Will County property tax in person?
faqs.a: At the Treasurer's office in the Will County Building, 302 N. Chicago Street in Joliet. The office accepts cash, check and credit card, and an after-hours drop box sits at the same building.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Will County assessment?
faqs.a: Yes. File a complaint for each parcel with the Board of Review, which opens its process every August. For 2026 the window ran from August 12 through September 14. Call (815) 740-4707 with questions.

faqs.q: How much is the Will County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: The cap is $8,000 off equalized assessed value for a general homestead, because Will borders Cook County. Seniors 65 and older can claim up to $8,000 under the senior exemption.

faqs.q: What if my Will County taxes were sold at the tax sale?
faqs.a: You can still redeem. Pay the County Clerk's tax redemption department before the redemption period ends, which the Treasurer describes as typically one to three years and the statute sets at three years from the sale, with exceptions.
